exam: A 28‑year‑old postpartum woman presents with RUQ pain, ascites, and a tender liver – what is your next diagnostic step? — Order Doppler ultrasound to assess hepatic vein flow.
How does Budd‑Chiari differ from right‑sided heart failure on examination? — BCS has tender hepatomegaly without peripheral edema; heart failure shows JVD and peripheral edema.

A patient with malaria develops sudden abdominal pain; labs show normal INR. What does this mean for anticoagulation? — Normal INR early does not rule out thrombosis; start heparin while investigating.
Why is warfarin alone inappropriate in acute hepatic vein thrombosis? — It does not provide immediate anticoagulation; heparin bridge is required.
What are the three clinical phases of Budd‑Chiari and their key features? — Acute (pain, ascites, encephalopathy), sub‑acute (moderate symptoms), chronic (portal hypertension, varices).
If Doppler ultrasound is unavailable, what is the alternative imaging modality and why? — Contrast CT or MRI, because they visualize the veins and any obstructing lesion.
What supportive measures reduce mortality in acute Budd‑Chiari? — Diuretics for ascites, lactulose for encephalopathy, antibiotics for infection, and early anticoagulation.
When is surgical shunting indicated over TIPS? — When TIPS is not feasible due to lack of expertise or equipment, or when anatomy precludes endovascular access.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The hepatic veins drain blood from the liver into the inferior vena cava. Obstruction causes Budd‑Chiari syndrome, a life‑threatening condition common in low‑resource settings with infections and hypercoagulable states.

b: Drain into IVC at the level of the diaphragm
sections.p: Three large hepatic veins (right, middle, left) empty into the inferior vena cava just above the liver. Their patency is essential for hepatic outflow; blockage leads to hepatic congestion, pain, and rapid liver failure.

b: Acute BCS: <2 weeks, severe pain, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy
sections.p: Budd‑Chiari syndrome (BCS) is defined by hepatic venous outflow obstruction. Diagnosis requires imaging or venography plus clinical features. In East Africa, common precipitants are thrombophilia (e.g., protein C/S deficiency), infections (malaria, schistosomiasis), pregnancy, and oral contraceptives.

b: Look for risk factors: recent pregnancy, HIV/TB therapy, herbal remedies with estrogenic effect
Assess for signs of liver failure: jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy
sections.p: Patients present with right‑upper‑quadrant pain, tender hepatomegaly, and rapidly accumulating ascites. Early recognition is vital because mortality exceeds 50 % without treatment.

t.b: Is there flow in the hepatic veins? – Absent or reversed flow confirms obstruction; if unavailable, proceed to bedside FAST for ascites and consider CT if possible.
What is the site and extent of blockage? – Shows thrombosis, membranous webs, or external compression; guides interventional planning.

t.a: Coagulation profile (PT/INR, platelets, protein C/S, antiphospholipid antibodies)
t.b: Is a hypercoagulable state present? – Abnormal results direct anticoagulation strategy.
How severe is hepatic injury? – Rising bilirubin, AST/ALT >5 × ULN, and low albumin indicate poor prognosis.

b: Start low‑molecular‑weight heparin (if no active bleeding) – prevents clot propagation
Consider oral vitamin K antagonists once stable – maintain INR 2‑3
If anticoagulation fails and facilities exist, perform TIPS to bypass obstruction
Supportive care: diuretics for ascites, lactulose for encephalopathy, broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection suspected
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, restore venous outflow, and support liver function. In low‑resource settings, anticoagulation and percutaneous trans‑jugular intra‑hepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) are often unavailable; surgical shunts or liver transplantation may be the only options.

b: Distinguish BCS from right‑sided heart failure by absence of peripheral edema and presence of tender hepatomegaly
Remember that a normal INR does not exclude early coagulopathy; repeat tests if clinical picture worsens

sections.p: Pitfalls include attributing ascites solely to cirrhosis, delaying Doppler imaging, and using warfarin without initial heparin bridging in acute thrombosis.
